I am an industrial food chemist. I actually have working knowledge of GMOs and I don't think Monsanto is the devil even though I don't work there. The average Voater is wildly and willingly ignorant of food policy and food science.

I meant to comment on this yesterday, but time got away from me. For starters, I do think there is a lot of misinformation being spread around. Full disclosure - I am anti-GMO. I don't think they give you cancer or eshew in an NWO age or anything like that, but the most commonly used GMOs (correct me if I am wrong) are used because they are round-ready and those manipulated for higher yields. This allows farmers, even encourages them, to grow massive monocultures that are food deserts for all other plants and animals. Most of these crops go towards feeding livestock a diet not even remotely close to that they would eat in nature which leads to sick animals that need to be on a steady diet of anti-biotics. The herbicide use also takes away a lot of food from insects that are beneficial to the crop. Killing weeds also causes compaction because the ground is no longer protected from the sun. I cannot tell you how depressed I get when I go to the local pumpkin patch in the fall and it feels like I am walking on cement, not soil.

I have also heard about golden rice, which is a rice modified to contain more nutrients. This is really silly because we strip the hull off rice removing most of the fiber and nutrients from the grain, which causes a population dependent on rice to become malnourished.

It's a cause and effect thing for me. All of our plants can be used like they have for thousands of years of human history to become productive, there is no need to mess with their genes in a lab IMO. Even the practice of simple cover-cropping, then having animals come in and clean up the plant debris (straw for example) leads to a healthier soil which leads to healthier plants.

Also Monsanto does suck, but it is mostly for legal reasons. Seed patenting and suing small farmers is a hard thing to defend for me. They own 95% of the seed stock in the first world - that's fucking scary. Their PR team is pretty weak too. Any arguments about "feeding the world" are really dumb since any starving populace is a result of corrupt local governments, not lack of food. And as discussed most of GMO crops go towards feeding livestock, which end up as unhealthy fast food hamburgers anyway.

I know this is your livelihood, and I'm not trying to discredit you, but if you have the time, I think you should take a look at Gabe Brown. With simple cover cropping and clever use of animals he has created a very healthy and productive farm that relies very minimally on any sort of -cide.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9yPjoh9YJMk

It is actually not my livelihood, I am an industrial food chemist. I work a lot with GMOs currently and in my last job I did plant genomic research. The problems you pointed out are problems, however, they are not directly resulted from GMOs. Farming practices can definitely be improved. Any time a major and new crop is introduced to a market, it tends to be over-used. For example, cotton in the antebellum south and wheat prior, and during, the dust bowl. With GMOs a farmer can plant them as they would any other crop, including responsibly and not responsibly. The same is true of soil quality. Soil quality is terrible in the region where I work. Many contributing factors exist for the low quality including overuse of fertilizers, overuse of the soil, improper drainage, over tilling, lack of cover crops, etc. GMOs simply cannot be singled out as the main factor in low soil quality.

Even if I buy that golden rice mildly improves the vitamin A content of rice, it still seems like a good idea. Given that the majority of children that are blinded or die from lack of vitamin A live in countries where rice is a food staple, it seems like a good idea to introduce that vitamin even in a small quantity. Golden rice is created to produce beta-carotene in the endosperm which is the part that humans eat. Rice naturally produces beta-carotene in the leaves, the GMO introduces the precursor into the edible parts.

The vast majority of apples that are eaten each year are produced via graphing. Do you also oppose the practice of graphing? It seems like you have a distinction without a definition.

Monsanto does have a bad PR team, I will give you that one. The legal argument though is flawed. Monsanto actually gets sued for contamination more than they sue, and they have a program where they will remove any contaminated fields at the farmers request using Monsanto's funds. The few major cases that were before the Supreme Court were all reasonable cases. One case was a farmer that went to a seed cleaner specifically to locate and keep Monsanto's seeds after his contract expired. Another was a challenge by groups saying you cannot patient DNA. Using the high estimate of over 870 legal actions or threats of legal action, this seems like a reasonable amount of legal action for a company that is located in the entire U.S.A and has been in operations for decades.

I am actually aware of Gabe Brown's ideas because my parents operate an organic apple and berry orchard. GMOs and biotechnology is not the only method of creating an effective agricultural system. However, both forms, conventional and organic, have trade offs that people have to admit exists. Organic agriculture requires massive amount of labor that is not sustainable on a level above a small to mid sized farm assuming current amounts of labor. Cuba is a fascinating example of organic agriculture because they needed to develop a whole system without any industrial chemicals during the blockade. I am watching Cuba's agriculture system closely to see what happens now that the blockage has loosened.

Thanks for the thoughtful comment. I still can never get on board with GMOs. It is a cause and effect thing for me (as stated), but it also comes down to this magic potion mentality. Need better yield? We have a seed for that. Sick of having consequences to spraying herbicides? We have a seed for that. Want to take your unstable monoculture and stretch it for miles? And huge stretches of the same crop need to be done away with, but they won't because people make good money from it, but it is ruining our soils. Small scale farms have their fair share of issues, but if they practice polycultures and working with the land, they are much more stable than any modified seed crop.

Your point on golden rice is not wrong, but I still feel it is unnecessary. I'm not against it, I'm pretty indifferent to it. I understand that apples don't produce the same variety from seed so graphing is the only way to get consistency, but if we planted more from seed we would end up with a better root systems and thousands of new varieties of apples. Then people could take the unpalatable apples and find a new way to use them - livestock feed, carpentry, cider, etc. This is what we used to do with them, why can't we still practice that?

The Cuba point is interesting. An optimist would say we can learn from them, but the realist in me thinks we will make them adopt our unsustainable practices just like the rest of the world. We will sell it to them the same way "but don't you want to double your Yield? Give us money and we will give you the perfect seed! We know more than nature." The state of modern agriculture saddens me greatly and I feel the only thing that will turn it around to be better for the environment will be a huge disaster. We need to focus more on soil building - not GMOs, not new sprays, not the superfood of the year. Just soil - everything will fall in place from there.

In closing, GMOs aren't the worst thing in agriculture, but as stated before I really don't think they bring anything beneficial that we don't already have for much cheaper. If we modified flowers to attract new pollinators or new plants to produce huge leaves that gave more biomass for soils I might get excited. But we just end up with useless shit like the arctic apple.
